e.etymology: The French form of Susanna, from Hebrew Shoshannah, lily. It was widely used for American girls in the middle of the 20th century.
namesakes: Suzanne Collins (author of The Hunger Games)
Suzanne Vega (singer-songwriter of Luka and Tom's Diner)

e.etymology: A surname Anglicized from Welsh ap Rhydderch, son of Rhydderch, an old Welsh personal name often glossed as reddish-brown. Rhydderch on its own is usually Anglicized as Roderick.
namesakes: Broderick Crawford (Oscar-winning actor of All the King's Men)

assoc.t: Matthew Broderick, star of Ferris Bueller's Day Off

e.etymology: From Sanskrit pranava, the name for the sacred syllable Om, from a root meaning to sound forth or praise.
A spelling of Madelyn, itself an alteration of Madeline with the -lyn ending. Madeline goes back through French Madeleine to Mary Magdalene, Mary of Magdala.

assoc.t: Madelyne Pryor, an X-Men villain in Marvel comics

e.etymology: For girls, a short form of Alison, Alyssa, Alexandra and similar names. For boys, a spelling of Arabic Ali, exalted or lofty, common in Egypt and West Africa.
namesakes: Aly Michalka (actress and half of the duo Aly & AJ)

e.etymology: A respelling of Lorelei, the name of a steep rock on the Rhine and of the siren said to lure boatmen onto it. The German name is usually explained as murmuring rock.

assoc.t: Lorelai Gilmore of Gilmore Girls (spelled Lorelai)

e.etymology: A compound of Anna, from Hebrew Channah, grace, and Lynn, in the pattern of Annalise and Annabeth.

An Armenian girls' name taken from Talin, a town in Armenia known for its 7th-century cathedral; Taleen is a common Armenian American spelling. A similar name has also become popular in the Arab world.

e.meaning: of the sage Atharvan; a name of Ganesha
e.etymology: From Sanskrit Atharvan, the ancient fire priest credited with the Atharvaveda, the fourth Veda. The name is also an epithet of Ganesha and is especially popular in Maharashtra.
A West African and French-influenced spelling of Muhammad, from Arabic muhammad, praised or praiseworthy, the name of the Prophet of Islam. This form is typical of Senegal, Guinea and Mali.

From Arabic Abu Bakr, literally father of a young camel, the byname of Muhammad's closest companion and the first caliph. Sunni Muslims give it in his honor; the one-word spelling is common in Central Asia.

A respelling of Guinevere, the Norman French form of Welsh Gwenhwyfar, from gwen, white or fair, and a second element meaning smooth or phantom. She is King Arthur's queen; Jennifer is the Cornish form.

assoc.t: Queen Guinevere of Arthurian legend (same sound)

e.etymology: An English surname from the many places called Hutton, from Old English hoh, a ridge or spur of land, and tun, settlement.

assoc.t: surname of model Lauren Hutton and actor Timothy Hutton

e.etymology: The English adjective honest, truthful and sincere, from Latin honestus, honorable. It joins modern virtue names such as True, Loyal and Justice.

assoc.t: The Honest Company, Jessica Alba's baby-care brand

e.etymology: A Hawaiian-style name in the family of Nalani (the heavens) and Kailani; lani is Hawaiian for sky, heaven or royalty. The Nai- form has become common only recently.
A 20th-century spelling of Jane, the English feminine of John, from Old French Jehanne and ultimately Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
Created for the heroine of an 1886 American novel by spelling alone backwards. It is sometimes also linked to a Cherokee name meaning black fox.
namesakes: Enola Holmes (Sherlock's sister in the Netflix films with Millie Bobby Brown)

assoc.t: Enola Gay, the B-29 that dropped the Hiroshima bomb

e.note: Enola Gay was the plane that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima; many adults still make that link.

e.etymology: The West African form of Maryam, the Arabic name of Mary, mother of Jesus, who is honored in the Quran. It is common in Senegal, Guinea, Gambia and Sierra Leone.
A modern American name that puts the Ry- of Ryan and Ryder with the -den ending of Aiden and Jayden. Ryden is also an English and Swedish surname.
A modern name in the family of Malia, Maleah and Malaya. Malia is the Hawaiian form of Maria; this spelling has no separate meaning on record.
Coined by Disney for Vanellope von Schweetz, the candy-kingdom racer in Wreck-It Ralph (2012). The name blends vanilla with Penelope.

assoc.t: Vanellope von Schweetz of Disney's Wreck-It Ralph

e.etymology: A Latin American name with no settled origin, close in sound to Caleb and Kaleb. Colombian vallenato singer Kaleth Morales (1984-2005) made it known.
A spelling of Cheyenne shaped by the name Anne. Cheyenne is the English name of a Great Plains nation, from Sahiyena, the Dakota Sioux word for them; it is also Wyoming's capital.

assoc.t: Cheyenne, the capital of Wyoming (same sound)
the Cheyenne, a Great Plains nation (same sound)

e.etymology: A short form of Chester, a surname from the English city, from Old English ceaster, a Roman town or fort, borrowed from Latin castra, camp.
An Irish surname, Tóibín, from the Norman de Saint Aubyn, a place named for St Albinus. As a first name it is also taken as a pet form of Tobias, from Hebrew Toviyah, God is good.
namesakes: Tobin Bell (Jigsaw in the Saw films)
Tobin Heath (US women's soccer World Cup winner)

e.etymology: A spelling of Nolan, from the Irish surname Ó Nualláin, descendant of Nuallán, a personal name from nuall, noble or famous.
From French Léonie, from Latin Leonia, the feminine of Leonius, built on leo, lion. It is a long-standing favorite in Germany and France.
A respelling of Berkeley, an English place name and surname from Old English beorc, birch, and leah, woodland clearing. It matches the spelling of Boston's Berklee College of Music.

assoc.t: Berklee College of Music in Boston
Berkeley, California, and its university (same sound)

e.etymology: A respelling of Emory, an English surname from the Norman name Amalric or Emmerich, built on Germanic ric, ruler, with a first element usually read as work.
A modern Indian name usually connected with Mira, after Mirabai, the 16th-century poet-saint devoted to Krishna; name lists gloss it as devotee of Krishna. It also sits close to Spanish Mireya.
The English word for the point of the sky directly overhead, and so any peak or high point. It came through Old French and Medieval Latin from Arabic samt ar-ra's, path over the head.

assoc.t: Zenith, the longtime American TV and radio maker

e.etymology: A modern name with no settled origin, close in sound to Lia, Liana and Kiara. Gamers know it from Liara T'Soni, the alien scientist in the Mass Effect series.

assoc.t: Liara T'Soni, alien companion in the Mass Effect games

e.note: On paper the name begins with the word liar, which classmates may notice.
